transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Lee. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Lee. Yeah, um, so what finally scared me into coming in is that I just keep making these really dumb technical mistakes at work. I'm a camera operator and video editor, and lately I've been doing things I absolutely know better than to do. 

Like, for example, we just got these new Sony FX6 cameras at the production company, which are incredible, honestly—the low-light sensor is just gorgeous, and it's so much lighter on my shoulder than the old rigs. My shoulder has been killing me lately, actually. I probably need to see a physical therapist, or maybe just get a better EZ rig for when we do documentary shoots. We did this one doc shoot in the woods last month and I swear I got eaten alive by mosquitoes because I forgot bug spray... wait, what was I saying? 

Oh, right, the mistakes. Yeah, so the media workflow is a little different now, and I keep labeling the camera cards wrong. Which is a huge deal in post-production. Or I'll completely miss a timecode note from the director. Just yesterday I was cutting this corporate piece—and corporate clients are the *worst*, they want everything so sterile, you know? They literally argued with me for twenty minutes once about the exact shade of blue in their logo. But anyway, I'll export a client cut for them and it'll have the completely wrong lower-third graphic on the screen. And the crazy part is, I *checked* it. I literally watched the export down before sending the review link, and I still somehow missed it. It's just getting really frustrating.
Have you always had trouble with focus and forgetfulness like this since childhood, or is this a new change for you recently?

No, it's definitely not new. It's been like this forever, honestly. Like, even way back in elementary school, my teachers were constantly moving my desk around. I was just always out of my seat, or I'd blurt out answers without raising my hand. 

Oh, and I had this one teacher, Mrs. Gable in third grade—she had those old wooden desks where you lift the top up, you know? Not the ones they have now where you just slide a plastic bin in. I used to keep so many random things in there. I actually found a fossil once on the playground and kept it in my desk for a whole year. I still love rocks, honestly. Whenever we do location scouts for shoots, I'm always looking at the ground to see if I can find cool stones. My director hates it because I always wander off into the dirt. 

But anyway, yeah, Mrs. Gable moved my desk right up next to hers because I was always bothering my classmates. Like, I'd just be talking to them or poking them or whatever before I even realized I was doing it. I think I sat next to this kid named Brian for exactly one day before she separated us. Brian actually just added me on LinkedIn the other day, which is wild because he's an accountant now. Who even uses LinkedIn to network with people they knew when they were eight? It's so weird. The interface on that site is terrible anyway, it's just people bragging about synergy. 

But... wait, yeah. Childhood. Definitely not a new thing.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a lifelong (since elementary school) pattern of both inattentive symptoms (careless mistakes despite checking work, difficulty sustaining focus, tangential/distractible thought process, forgetfulness of task details) and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (out-of-seat behavior, blurting answers, impulsively touching/talking to classmates, current-day wandering off during work tasks). Symptoms began before age 12, have persisted across settings (school and current workplace), and are currently causing functional impairment (repeated costly errors in professional video editing work). This combined presentation of both inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptom clusters meeting duration and cross-situational criteria supports ADHD, Combined Type (F90.0).
